title: Eat less, age slower: the 20-year monkey study that put a diet myth to the test

study.citation: Colman, R. J. et al. (2009), "Caloric Restriction Delays Disease Onset and Mortality in Rhesus Monkeys", Science 325(5937), 201-204

tldr: Trimming a monkey's calories by 30 percent for twenty years, while keeping its nutrition complete, roughly tripled its odds of avoiding an age-related death and cut its diabetes, cancer, and heart disease.

sections.body: Everyone wants more healthy years. For decades, one trick reliably stretched lifespan in the lab: feed an animal less. Cut the calories of a rat, a fly, or a worm by roughly a third, keep its nutrition complete, and it tends to live longer and fall ill later. But those creatures are far from us. A mouse and a person share plenty of biology, yet a mouse lives about two years and a human lives eighty. Would the same hungry bargain hold in a primate whose body and lifespan actually resemble ours? A team in Wisconsin spent two decades finding out.

Beginning in 1989, researchers at the Wisconsin National Primate Research Center followed 76 adult rhesus monkeys, a species that can live into its thirties. Half kept eating their normal, individually measured portions. The other half had their calories trimmed by 30 percent, eased in gradually over three months so no monkey ever went hungry overnight. Both groups received the same complete vitamins, minerals, and protein, so the one real difference was total energy. Then the scientists simply watched, for twenty years, tracking who developed diabetes, cancer, heart disease, and brain shrinkage, and who was still alive.

The lean-fed monkeys aged more gently. Among the animals studied, 37 percent of the normally fed monkeys died of age-related causes, against 13 percent of the restricted group, roughly a threefold gap. Diabetes essentially vanished under restriction: several normally fed monkeys developed it, while the dieting monkeys stayed metabolically healthy. Cancer and heart disease each fell by about half. Their brains even held onto more gray matter in regions tied to movement and control. Side by side in photographs, the calorie-trimmed monkeys looked visibly younger, with fuller fur and less frailty, than their well-fed cage-mates.

This was the first strong sign that a rule seen in worms and mice might reach all the way up to a long-lived primate close to us. If simply eating less could delay diabetes, cancer, and heart disease in a monkey, then aging itself might be more adjustable than it looks, a dial we can turn rather than a fixed clock. The result poured fuel on a search that continues today: for drugs and eating patterns that copy the effects of restriction without the constant hunger. The excitement around metformin, rapamycin, and time-restricted eating traces part of its lineage to findings like this one.

Three years later, a parallel study at the National Institute on Aging cut calories the same way and found no clear survival benefit, which set off a long argument. The likely culprit was the comparison group: the government study's normally fed monkeys ate a tightly portioned, healthier diet, so they were already mildly restricted, and that shrank the gap. In 2017 the two teams pooled their data and agreed that restriction does help, with the payoff depending on diet quality and the age you begin. And monkeys are still not people. A human sustaining a 30 percent cut for decades is a hard, largely untested ask.

terms.def: Eating meaningfully fewer calories (here about 30 percent less) while still getting all the vitamins, minerals, and protein the body needs.
A death caused by a disease of aging, such as cancer, diabetes, or heart failure, rather than by injury or infection.
The parts of the brain packed with nerve-cell bodies that do much of its processing; it tends to shrink as we grow older.

takeaways: Cutting a monkey's calories by 30 percent, with full nutrition kept intact, roughly tripled its odds of avoiding an age-related death over twenty years.
The diet slashed diabetes, cancer, and heart disease and even preserved brain tissue, hinting that the pace of aging can be nudged.

A rival study found no survival edge because its control monkeys were already eating lean, and a later joint reanalysis still backed restriction — a reminder that in diet research the comparison group can decide the result.

quiz.q: What was the single main difference between the two groups of monkeys?
choices: The restricted group ate 30 percent fewer calories while getting the same complete nutrition
The restricted group ate an entirely different type of food
The restricted group exercised far more
The restricted group was much younger at the start
quiz.why: Both groups received identical vitamins, minerals, and protein; the only real change was total energy. The restricted monkeys had their calories trimmed by about 30 percent, phased in gradually, which let researchers tie any difference in aging to calories alone.

quiz.q: What happened to age-related deaths in the calorie-restricted monkeys?
choices: They stayed exactly the same as the control group
They fell to roughly a third of the control group's rate
quiz.why: About 37 percent of the normally fed monkeys died of age-related causes, versus roughly 13 percent of the restricted group — close to a threefold difference, alongside less diabetes, cancer, and heart disease.

quiz.q: Why did a second monkey study at first seem to contradict this one?
choices: It used mice instead of monkeys
Its comparison monkeys were already eating a lean, portioned diet, which shrank the difference
It only lasted a few weeks
It fed both groups unlimited junk food
quiz.why: The National Institute on Aging's control monkeys ate a tightly portioned, healthier diet, so they were effectively mildly restricted already. That narrowed the gap and hid a survival benefit; a 2017 joint reanalysis of both studies concluded that restriction does help.
